title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
subject: Science

notes.heading: Chemical Reaction
notes.text: A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances change into new substances with different properties. The substances that take part in a chemical reaction are called reactants, and the new substances formed are called products.
points: Example When magnesium burns in oxygen:

Here:
Reactants = Magnesium + Oxygen
Product = Magnesium oxide

A chemical reaction may be identified by:
Change in colour
Change in temperature
Formation of a gas
Formation of a precipitate
Change in physical state

notes.heading: Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation is a short representation of a chemical reaction using the symbols and chemical formulae of the substances involved.
points: For example:
This represents the reaction:

So, remember:
Chemical Reaction = Actual process
Chemical Equation = Symbolic representation of the process
notes.example:
\[\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}\]

Magnesium + Oxygen ⟶ Magnesium oxide

notes.heading: 1.1 Chemical Equations
notes.text: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction. Instead of writing the names of substances, we use their chemical symbols and formulae.
points: Example The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water can be written as:
Using chemical formulae:
Here: • \(\ce{H2}\) and \(\ce{O2}\) are the reactants. • \(\ce{H2O}\) is the product. • The arrow ⟶ means “forms” or “gives”.
A chemical equation gives us information about which substances react and which substances are formed.

notes.heading: 1.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using the symbols and formulae of the substances involved.
points: Steps for writing a chemical equation
numberedPoints: Write the reactants on the left-hand side.
Write the products on the right-hand side.
Separate reactants and products using an arrow ⟶.
notes.example: Example When magnesium reacts with oxygen, magnesium oxide is formed. In words: Magnesium + Oxygen ⟶ Magnesium oxide Using chemical formulae: \[\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}\] Here: \(\ce{Mg}\), \(\ce{O2}\) = Reactants \(\ce{MgO}\) = Product

notes.heading: Skeletal Chemical Equation
notes.text: This equation is called a skeletal chemical equation because it represents the reaction but is not balanced.
points: General form
Remember: Reactants are written on the left-hand side, and products are written on the right-hand side.

notes.heading: 1.1.2 Balanced Chemical Equations
notes.text: A balanced chemical equation is an equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides of the equation. This is based on the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
points: Example Consider:

Count the atoms:
Element    Left side    Right side
Mg         1            1
O          2            1
The number of oxygen atoms is not equal, so the equation is not balanced.
We balance it by putting suitable numbers called coefficients before the formulae:
Now: Element Left side Right side Mg 2 2 O 2 2 Therefore, the equation is balanced.

notes.heading: Important Rule
notes.text: While balancing an equation, we change only the coefficients, not the chemical formulae. For example, we can write:
points: But we should not change \(\ce{H2O}\) into another formula just to balance the equation.
In short Number of atoms of each element on LHS = Number of atoms on RHS
A balanced chemical equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.

notes.heading: 1.2 Types of Chemical Reactions
notes.text: Chemical reactions can be classified into different types depending on how the reactants change into products. The main types are:
points: These reactions have different patterns, which help us identify them easily.

notes.heading: 1.2.1 Combination Reaction
notes.text: A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form a single product.
points: General form
Here, two or more reactants combine to form only one product.
Example 1: Formation of Calcium Oxide Calcium reacts with oxygen to form calcium oxide:
Here, calcium and oxygen combine to form one product, calcium oxide.

notes.heading: Combination Reaction — Examples 2 and 3
notes.text: Example 2: Formation of Water Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water: Example 3: Burning of Coal Carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide:
points: Again, two reactants combine to form one product.
Key Point The easiest way to identify a combination reaction is:
So, many substances combine to give one substance.
notes.example:
\[\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}\]

\[\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}\]

\[\ce{Two or more reactants -> One product}\]

notes.heading: 1.2.2 Decomposition Reaction
notes.text: A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. It is the opposite of a combination reaction.
points: General form
Here, one reactant breaks down to form two or more products.
Example 1: Decomposition of Calcium Carbonate On heating calcium carbonate, it decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: Here, Δ represents heat.
Example 2: Decomposition of Water Water can be decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen by passing electricity through it:
Types of Decomposition Reactions Decomposition can occur due to: • Heat → Thermal decomposition
Key Point One reactant ⟶ Two or more products So, in a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks down into simpler substances.

notes.heading: Types of Decomposition Reactions
notes.text: Decomposition can occur due to:
points: • Electricity → Electrolytic decomposition • Light → Photolytic decomposition

notes.heading: 1.2.3 Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
points: General form
Here, element \(A\) is more reactive than \(B\), so \(A\) displaces \(B\) from the compound \(BC\).
Example Zinc reacts with copper sulphate solution:
Here: • Zinc \((Zn)\) is more reactive than copper \((Cu)\). • Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate. • Zinc sulphate and copper are formed.
Another example Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate:
Key Point More reactive element + Compound ⟶ New compound + Less reactive element
Remember: A displacement reaction involves the displacement of one element by another more reactive element.
notes.example:
\[\ce{A + BC -> AC + B}\]

\[\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}\]

\[\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}\]

notes.heading: 1.2.4 Double Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A double displacement reaction is a reaction in which two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.
points: General form
Here, the ions of the two compounds exchange places.
Example When sodium sulphate reacts with barium chloride:
Here: • \(\ce{Na2SO4}\) and \(\ce{BaCl2}\) are the reactants. • \(\ce{BaSO4}\) and \(\ce{NaCl}\) are the products. • \(\ce{BaSO4}\) is an insoluble white solid called a precipitate.
Therefore, this reaction is also called a precipitation reaction.
Key Point Two compounds ⟶ Two new compounds The compounds exchange their ions during the reaction.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction
notes.text: Oxidation and reduction are chemical processes that often occur together in a reaction.

notes.heading: Oxidation
notes.text: Oxidation can be understood as:
points: • Addition of oxygen • Removal of hydrogen • Loss of electrons
For example:
Copper combines with oxygen, so copper is oxidised.

notes.heading: Reduction
notes.text: Reduction can be understood as:
points: • Removal of oxygen • Addition of hydrogen • Gain of electrons
For example:
Oxygen is removed from copper oxide, so copper oxide is reduced.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction Together
notes.text: When oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction, the reaction is called a redox reaction.
points: For example:
• \(\ce{CuO}\) loses oxygen → Reduction • \(\ce{H2}\) gains oxygen → Oxidation
Thus, oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
Easy way to remember Oxidation = Addition of Oxygen Reduction = Removal of Oxygen And: Oxidation + Reduction = Redox Reaction

notes.heading: 1.3 Effects of Oxidation Reactions in Everyday Life
notes.text: Oxidation reactions do not occur only in laboratories. They also happen around us in everyday life.
points: Two important effects of oxidation are: • Corrosion • Rancidity
These processes can cause damage to metals and food.

notes.heading: 1.3.1 Corrosion
notes.text: Corrosion is the process in which a metal is gradually destroyed or damaged due to reactions with substances present in the environment, such as oxygen, moisture, acids, etc.
points: Example: Rusting of Iron Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture present in air to form rust.
Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide. \(\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}\) The reddish-brown coating seen on iron objects is rust.
Other Examples of Corrosion • Copper develops a green coating of basic copper carbonate. • Silver develops a black coating of silver sulphide.
Prevention of Corrosion Corrosion can be prevented by protecting the metal from contact with air and moisture. Common methods include: • Painting • Oiling or greasing • Galvanisation • Alloying
Key Point Corrosion = Gradual damage of a metal due to environmental reactions Rusting of iron is one of the most common examples of corrosion.

notes.heading: 1.3.2 Rancidity
notes.text: Rancidity is the process in which food containing fats and oils gets oxidised, causing an unpleasant smell and taste.
points: For example, when oily food is left exposed to air for a long time, it may develop a bad smell and taste. This happens because the fats and oils in the food undergo oxidation.

Prevention of Rancidity Rancidity can be prevented or slowed down by: • Adding antioxidants to food. • Keeping food in airtight containers to prevent contact with oxygen. • Refrigerating food, which slows down oxidation. • Packing some foods using nitrogen gas instead of oxygen.
Example Chips packets are often filled with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen prevents the oils in the chips from coming into contact with oxygen and becoming rancid.
Key Point Rancidity = Oxidation of fats and oils causing unpleasant smell and taste

summary: The chapter explains chemical reactions, chemical equations, balancing of equations, types of chemical reactions, oxidation and reduction, redox reactions, and the effects of oxidation in everyday life such as corrosion and rancidity.
